title: The exit interview
setting: An HR manager talks to someone who has handed in their notice.

lines.t: Thanks for doing this. There's nothing to lose by being direct.
All right. It wasn't the money, if that's the first question.
It was, actually. So what was it?
The shifts. They're published on Friday for the following Monday.
And that made life outside work impossible to plan.
I cancelled the same course three times. Eventually I stopped booking things.
Did you raise it with your line manager?
Twice. I was told it's how the department works.
That's useful, and I'm sorry it took your resignation for me to hear it.
Fix it for the others and I'll consider that a good outcome.

title: Asking for a pay rise
setting: An employee raises salary in a performance review.

lines.t: Before we finish, I'd like to talk about my salary.
Go ahead.
I've taken on the reporting and I'm training two new starters.
Both true. What figure did you have in mind?
Twelve per cent, which brings me in line with the market for this role.
That's above what I can approve alone. I'd need to build a case.
What would make that case stronger?
Numbers. How much time the new reporting saves the team each month.
I can put that together this week.
Do that, and I'll take it to the head of department in the next cycle.

title: Ninety applicants
setting: One open job has produced far more applications than anyone can read.

lines.t: Ninety applicants for one vacancy.
Because the job posting says 'competitive salary' and nothing else.
We never put numbers in.
Then we get ninety people, and eighty of them want a different job.
How do we cut it down?
A fifteen-minute screening call each. That gets us to a shortlist of six by Friday.
And then?
A competency-based interview. Ask what they actually did last March. Hypothetical questions get hypothetical answers.
Everybody says they're a team player.
So ask about the last time they disagreed with a manager. Then a reference check before the offer letter goes anywhere.
And if our first choice says no?
We go to the second name. That's why you interview six and not two, and why the hire is decided before anyone celebrates.

title: What's actually in it
setting: A new employee reads the paperwork before signing it.

lines.t: Before I sign, can we go through the contract of employment?
Of course. It's permanent. The fixed-term contract we discussed in July is off the table.
What's in the benefits package?
Pension scheme from day one, health insurance after probation, twenty-five days of holiday.
And overtime?
Paid at 150%, or taken as time off. Most people here take the time.
Is there a bonus?
Once a year, tied to the company result. I'd rather you didn't plan your life around it.
When is a pay rise discussed?
At twelve months, in writing, with your manager.
And if something looks wrong on my payslip?
You come to me that week. We had a temp last year who said nothing for four months, and putting it right took longer than it should have.

title: Nobody takes it
setting: A department with suspiciously low absence figures.

lines.t: Your team's absence rate is the lowest in the company.
That sounds like good news.
Four of them have annual leave they haven't touched since last summer.
They keep saying they'll take it later.
Later is how people end up owed six weeks in December.
What about Mira's parental leave?
It starts in March and she's back in October. We'll need a temp from February.
And Stoyan has been ill twice this month.
Sick pay covers him, and nobody should be at a desk with a fever.
Then I'll put flexitime in writing for the whole team, and anyone who works a Saturday takes time off in lieu the week after.

title: The survey nobody answered
setting: People are leaving and the official figures say everyone is happy.

lines.t: Staff turnover is 22%. Last year it was 12%.
And the engagement survey says everyone is fine.
Eleven per cent answered it.
Then it tells us one thing only: people don't trust it.
Who left?
Four from your department. Two said workload, one said burnout, one said nothing at all.
Retention costs less than hiring. I say it in every meeting.
And the meeting is where it stops. What changed after the last survey?
Nothing anybody could see.
Then start with one visible thing. Work-life balance improves the day somebody senior leaves at five.
And the equal opportunities training?
Do it properly or leave it alone. Diversity and inclusion on a slide with nothing behind it damages job satisfaction faster than silence does.

title: Two weeks after the promotion
setting: Somebody resigns immediately after being given a bigger job.

lines.t: Ivo handed in his notice this morning.
Was it a surprise?
Completely. He'd just been given the Varna project.
Then his resignation is telling us something, and the exit interview is where we find out what.
Will he be honest?
More honest than he's been in a year. Ask what nearly kept him here.
Should I try to match the offer?
Only if you'd have paid it last month, before he resigned.
And the position itself?
It stays open. Redundancy means the job disappears, dismissal means we ended it, and neither applies here. Somebody got a better offer.

title: Three pages, handwritten
setting: A formal complaint arrives about a supervisor, with a second problem behind it.

lines.t: Somebody has raised a grievance against a supervisor.
In writing, or in conversation?
In writing. Three pages.
Then the disciplinary procedure starts today and we follow every step of it.
Does that mean somebody is guilty?
It means we investigate. Half of these end with nobody at fault.
And if it is misconduct?
A written warning stays on file for twelve months, and the code of conduct says what happens if it repeats.
He also forwarded an email to the regulator.
That's whistleblowing and it's protected. Nothing about his job changes because of it, and if anything does, we have a far bigger problem than the original complaint.
Understood. Where do I start?
You don't. I do, because you manage the supervisor.

title: Where does this go
setting: An employee asks what the next three years look like.

lines.t: I want to know where this job goes in three years.
Then let's draw the career path and see whether it exists here.
That sounds like it might not.
It might not, and I'd rather you heard that from me than worked it out slowly.
What's missing?
Two things. You've never managed anyone, and you don't read financial reports.
So that's the skills gap.
That's all of it. Learning and development covers a course for the second one.
And the first?
A mentor, somebody two steps ahead of you. We can upskill you where you are, or reskill you for a different role if that's what you'd rather have.
